info.title: Sizing and reserving crash kernel memory

abstract.para: Before &kdump; can capture a crash dump, a dedicated area of memory must be reserved for the capture kernel. Use kdumptool calibrate to determine a suitable size, or set it manually if the automatic value is not sufficient. kdumptool is part of the kdump package. See if it is not installed yet.

section.title: Using the automatically calculated size
section.para: By default, KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL in /etc/sysconfig/kdump is set to auto. With this setting, kdumptool commandline derives the crash kernel memory size from kdumptool calibrate automatically. You do not need to calculate or set anything manually to get started. Run the calibration tool directly to see the values it would use:

example.title: Determining the recommended crash kernel memory size
example.screen: Total: 4095 Low: 72 High: 394 MinLow: 72 MaxLow: 666 MinHigh: 0 MaxHigh: 2048

section.para: All values are given in megabytes. Low is the recommended reservation in the DMA32 zone (memory up to the 4 GiB mark). High is the recommended reservation from the remaining available memory. MinLow/ MaxLow and MinHigh/MaxHigh give the valid range around those recommendations.

note.title: Calibrated values depend on the system
note.para: The exact numbers returned by kdumptool calibrate depend on the amount of RAM and the hardware configuration of the machine it runs on. Always run it on the target system itself rather than reusing values from another machine.

section.title: Crash kernel memory formats
section.para: When you set KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL manually, the value is either auto or one or more crashkernel= options in one of these formats:

listitem.para: crashkernel=SIZE[@OFFSET] reserves a fixed amount of memory, for example crashkernel=256M. The optional offset is the physical address where the reserved area starts. A suitable size is the sum of the Low and High values from kdumptool calibrate.

crashkernel=SIZE_LOWM,low crashkernel=SIZE_HIGHM,high reserves one area below the 4 GiB mark and one from the remaining memory, for example crashkernel=72M,low crashkernel=394M,high. This is the form that auto produces on &x86-64;.

crashkernel=RANGE1:SIZE1[,RANGE2:SIZE2,...][@OFFSET] reserves a size that depends on the amount of installed RAM. Each range has the form START-[END], where the start is inclusive and the end is exclusive. For example, crashkernel=512M-2G:64M,2G-:128M reserves nothing on systems with less than 512 MiB of RAM, 64 MiB on systems with 512 MiB up to but not including 2 GiB, and 128 MiB on systems with 2 GiB or more.

section.remark: ssarkar: the LUN-based sizing formula above is carried forward from the SLE 15 tuning guide (xml/tuning_kexec.xml in doc-sle) and was not independently re-verified against current kernel/kdump documentation this session — the sizing mechanics are kernel-internal (DMA32 zone reservation) and unlikely to have changed with SLE 16, but this should get a second look, ideally against `man 7 kdump` on a system with multiple real LUNs attached, before treating it as fully confirmed.
section.para: The Low value covers the memory that 32-bit-only devices require, including 64 MiB for DMA32 bounce buffers. If the system has no 32-bit-only devices, the default of 72 MiB is normally sufficient. If the drivers for your devices make many reservations in the DMA32 zone, raise Low as well. There is no formula for this, so finding the right size is a process of trial and error. On NUMA machines, more Low memory can appear to be needed. Adding numa=off to KDUMP_COMMANDLINE_APPEND boots the capture kernel without NUMA, so that normal kernel allocations do not use Low memory.
section.remark: ssarkar: the Low value guidance above (bounce buffers, 72 MiB default, trial and error, numa=off) is carried forward from the SLE 15 tuning guide. The 72 MiB default was confirmed with kdumptool calibrate on the SLES 16 test systems; the 64 MiB bounce buffer figure and the numa=off behavior were not independently verified.

section.title: Reducing the required memory by excluding unused devices on &zseries;
section.para: Depending on the number of available devices, the calculated crash kernel memory may not be sufficient. Instead of increasing the value, you can limit the number of devices that the capture kernel sees. This lowers the memory the reservation needs.

step.para: Generate a cio_ignore stanza that ignores all devices except the ones that are currently active or in use:

This command activates the blocklist immediately and replaces any existing blocklist. Unused devices are not purged, so they still appear in the channel subsystem, but channel devices that you add afterward (with CP ATTACH under z/VM, or by a dynamic I/O configuration change in an LPAR) are treated as blocked. To keep the original setting, run cio_ignore -l first and revert to that state after running cio_ignore -u -k.

section.title: Applying a changed reservation
section.para: After changing KDUMP_CRASHKERNEL, a full system reboot is required, since the crash kernel memory reservation is applied at boot time. See for how the new value is picked up.
